title: Bookshop ordering policy
brief:
Write an inventory review for a small bookshop owner allocating $900 of advance-order cash among four categories. Fictional history covers the winter buying window in two successive years. Each pair lists units received, units sold within 90 days, and customer requests while sold out. Local guides: (40, 36, 7), (45, 44, 15). Puzzles: (60, 42, 0), (55, 47, 3). Cookbooks: (50, 31, 0), (48, 34, 0). Graphic novels: (55, 43, 4), (65, 59, 9). Unit costs are $9, $11, $16, and $10 respectively. Order at least 10 per category. Analyze sell-through and missed demand, justify a purchase plan, and discuss how its risks change if demand falls.

Aim for 1,200 to 1,800 words. Return the complete original work directly in your answer. Do not sign or identify yourself. Do not use tools.

8d436c56aa0cd257.text:
I would spend the $900 on **33 local guides, 13 puzzles, 10 cookbooks, and 30 graphic novels**. Local guides get the most copies because they nearly sold out the latest shipment within 90 days, drew the most requests while unavailable, and cost the least to buy. Graphic novels get slightly more cash than guides because they cost a dollar more per copy and have the highest recorded unit sales. Puzzles earn a modest order above the minimum after a stronger second winter. Cookbooks stay at ten because they tie up the most cash per copy and have shown the least pressure on supply.

| Category | Copies to order | Unit cost | Advance cash |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Local guides | 33 | $9 | $297 |
| Puzzles | 13 | $11 | $143 |
| Cookbooks | 10 | $16 | $160 |
| Graphic novels | 30 | $10 | $300 |
| **Total** | **86** | | **$900** |

### What the two winters show

Sell-through measures the share of received units sold within 90 days. It matters alongside the sales count because the shop changed its order quantities between winters. Selling more from a larger shipment can simply reflect better availability. Selling more from a smaller shipment gives the owner a different reason to reconsider the next order.

| Category | First winter, sold / received | Second winter, sold / received | Requests while sold out, first → second |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Local guides | 36 / 40 = 90.0% | 44 / 45 = 97.8% | 7 → 15 |
| Puzzles | 42 / 60 = 70.0% | 47 / 55 = 85.5% | 0 → 3 |
| Cookbooks | 31 / 50 = 62.0% | 34 / 48 = 70.8% | 0 → 0 |
| Graphic novels | 43 / 55 = 78.2% | 59 / 65 = 90.8% | 4 → 9 |

**Local guides.** The shop received five more guides in the second winter and sold eight more. Only one of the 45 copies remained unsold at day 90, yet staff recorded 15 requests while guides were unavailable. That combination makes guides the first place I would put discretionary cash. It also makes title selection consequential. A copy of one neighborhood guide can remain on the shelf while customers repeatedly ask for another. If the request log names titles, those names should carry more weight in choosing the 33 copies than a general increase across every guide on the list.

**Puzzles.** Puzzles posted the largest gain in sell-through, up 15.5 percentage points. The shop bought five fewer units and sold five more, reducing the unsold balance from 18 to eight. The three requests in the second winter are the first recorded sign that availability cost the category some business. An order of 13 may look small against 47 recent sales, and it is. The reason to hold it there is the competition for cash from two categories with stronger evidence of shortages. The improvement earns puzzles three copies above the minimum and makes them worth watching early in the season.

**Cookbooks.** Cookbook sales rose from 31 to 34 even as receipts fell by two. That is a reason to keep a credible selection. Still, 14 of the latest 48 copies remained unsold after 90 days, and neither winter produced a request while cookbooks were sold out. At cost, those 14 copies represented $224 still on the shelf at the end of the measured window. They could sell later, but that cash was unavailable for another purchase in the meantime. Even the minimum order of ten takes $160, more than the entire proposed puzzle order. I would use those ten places for titles with a record of selling in this shop.

**Graphic novels.** The additional ten copies received in the second winter supported 16 additional sales. The unsold balance fell from 12 to six, while requests rose from four to nine. Graphic novels therefore combine the highest sales volume with evidence that customers would have bought a different mix or more copies of particular titles. They merit 30 units and the largest dollar allocation. The main risk of ordering only 30 is clear from the first winter alone, when the shop sold 43. If this advance order has to last the full season, some customers will likely encounter gaps even if sales ease from their recent high.

### How to read missed demand

A request while sold out is good evidence that availability mattered to a customer. Its value as a sales forecast depends on what happened next. One reader might ask twice, accept a substitute, or return to buy the requested book after a delivery. Other readers may see an empty space and leave without asking. The 15 guide requests justify giving guides priority, but adding all 15 to the 44 sales and forecasting exactly 59 purchases would imply more precision than the records support.

The category totals also leave open *when* the gaps occurred. Nine requests for the same graphic novel early in winter would argue for buying that title more deeply. Nine requests spread over nine titles would argue for a broader selection. With limited cash, that distinction can matter as much as shifting a few dollars between categories. For this order, I would first match available title-level requests to sales records, especially for guides and graphic novels, where the shop has evidence of shortages in both winters.

### Why this mix fits the cash limit

Buying ten of everything accounts for $460 before the owner makes a discretionary choice. The remaining $440 buys 23 extra guides for $207, three extra puzzles for $33, and 20 extra graphic novels for $200. This leaves guides and graphic novels almost level in total cash exposure, while the lower guide cost buys three more opportunities to serve a customer. The plan uses the full budget and meets all four minimums.

The constraint is substantial. The shop sold 184 units across these categories in the latest winter, compared with 86 units in this order. I have treated the quantities as advance purchases and assumed no particular amount of carryover stock. If last winter’s unsold copies are still available, they count toward what customers can find this winter, especially among cookbooks and puzzles. Selling prices and margins are also unknown, so the case for the allocation rests on observed sales, shortages, and purchase cost. A profit-maximizing order would require knowing what the shop earns when each unit sells.

### What changes if demand falls

As a simple stress test, suppose each category’s demand falls 25% from its second-winter recorded sales. That gives roughly 33 guide sales, 35 puzzle sales, 26 cookbook sales, and 44 graphic novel sales. Assuming the right titles and no carryover, the proposed guides would just cover that level. The other three orders would still fall short of it. A broad decline of that size would therefore ease the risk of turning customers away, while leaving little reason to expect a large pile of unsold stock from this purchase. The shop could nevertheless sell out of a popular title while slower titles remain.

At a 40% decline on the same basis, the picture changes first for guides. Demand would be about 26 guides against an order of 33, leaving roughly seven copies, or $63 at cost, still on hand after 90 days. Graphic novel demand would be about 35 against 30 ordered. Puzzle and cookbook demand would also remain above their order quantities. Guides thus carry the greatest near-term exposure to a uniform downturn, even though they had the best historical sell-through. The owner has chosen to cover a larger share of recent guide sales because the evidence of missed demand was strongest there.

An uneven decline calls for a different response. If early sales show guides weakening while graphic novels continue to move, the owner should use any later buying cash on the specific novels customers are asking for. If every category slows, the better course is to sell through the advance order before committing more cash. A weekly check of copies sold, copies on hand, and requests by title would give the owner enough information to distinguish those situations. That is particularly important for an 86-unit purchase, where a handful of requests for one title can justify a reorder even during a softer winter overall.

783d729ec2a0b971.text:
# Winter advance-order inventory review

Put **$306 into 34 local guides, $154 into 14 puzzles, $160 into 10 cookbooks, and $280 into 28 graphic novels**. The order uses the full $900 and meets the 10-unit minimum in every category. Local guides and graphic novels receive about 65% of the budget because they had the strongest recent sell-through and together accounted for 24 of the 27 requests recorded during stockouts in the latest winter. Puzzles earn a modest order after a stronger second year. Cookbooks stay at the minimum because they have the highest unit cost and left the most stock at the end of both 90-day windows.

## What the two winters show

Sell-through is the number of units sold within 90 days divided by the number received. The units left in the table are receipts minus recorded sales for that winter. Current shelf counts would need to be checked separately.

| Category | First winter sell-through | Second winter sell-through | Units left, first → second | Stockout requests, first → second |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Local guides | 90.0% (36 of 40) | 97.8% (44 of 45) | 4 → 1 | 7 → 15 |
| Puzzles | 70.0% (42 of 60) | 85.5% (47 of 55) | 18 → 8 | 0 → 3 |
| Cookbooks | 62.0% (31 of 50) | 70.8% (34 of 48) | 19 → 14 | 0 → 0 |
| Graphic novels | 78.2% (43 of 55) | 90.8% (59 of 65) | 12 → 6 | 4 → 9 |

Across all four categories, 90-day sell-through rose from 74.1% to 86.4%, and recorded stockout requests rose from 11 to 27. The same two categories led on both measures in the second winter. Local guides sold eight more copies on five additional receipts and finished with just one unit left. Graphic novels sold 16 more copies on 10 additional receipts, the largest unit-sales gain of any category. Both categories sold through a greater share of a larger buy while attracting more requests during stockouts.

Puzzles also improved. They sold five more units on five fewer receipts, cutting 90-day leftovers from 18 to eight. The three stockout requests give some reason to buy above the minimum, especially for titles that prompted those requests. Cookbooks sold three more units on two fewer receipts, but 14 of 48 remained after 90 days and there were no recorded requests. A cookbook costs $16, so a speculative copy ties up almost as much cash as a local guide and a graphic novel combined.

Treat the request counts as evidence of demand the shop could not immediately serve. Adding requests to sales gives 59 for guides, 50 for puzzles, 34 for cookbooks, and 68 for graphic novels in the second winter. Those sums are useful for seeing where shortages may have mattered, but they are rough measures of customer interest. A customer might ask twice, buy a substitute, or return later and appear in the sales count. Stockout requests and leftover stock can also coexist if popular titles sell out while slower titles remain on the shelf. The order should therefore put extra copies into the specific titles customers asked for, where the shop has that detail.

## How to spend the $900

| Category | Advance order | Unit cost | Cash allocated |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Local guides | 34 | $9 | $306 |
| Puzzles | 14 | $11 | $154 |
| Cookbooks | 10 | $16 | $160 |
| Graphic novels | 28 | $10 | $280 |
| **Total** | **86** | | **$900** |

The four minimum orders cost $460. Of the remaining $440, the plan puts $216 into 24 additional guides, $180 into 18 additional graphic novels, and $44 into four additional puzzles. The two winters give guides the strongest case for depth. They had the highest sell-through in each year and drew 15 stockout requests in the latest window. At $9 a copy, they also let the shop put more units on the shelf per dollar than any other category.

Graphic novels get the second-largest allocation. Their latest sales of 59 units give a 28-copy advance order substantial room if demand cools, and the nine stockout requests make a case for ordering more deeply into confirmed favorites. Fourteen puzzles give the shop room to act on the improvement in recent sales while keeping the cash commitment modest. For cookbooks, the 10-copy minimum preserves a buying presence. With 14 units remaining after the last window, the shop should check which titles are still available before placing the order and use the new copies where they fill gaps.

This is an advance-order allocation. Recent sales exceeded the proposed order in every category, so opening inventory and any later replenishment will determine how much of a strong winter the shop can serve. Check current stock by title before committing the order, especially if the remaining copies are concentrated in slower sellers. The budget and demand figures support a judgment about how quickly the shop may recover its inventory cash. A profit comparison would also require selling prices, margins, and any return terms.

## How the risk changes if demand falls

Using the latest winter’s recorded sales as a baseline, the guide order is the most exposed to a downturn. Sales could fall about 23% before category demand dipped below the 34 copies ordered. The corresponding cushion is about 53% for graphic novels and about 70% for both puzzles and cookbooks. Cookbooks have a large cushion in this comparison because the order is small relative to last winter’s sales. Their downside is the $16 tied up in each unsold copy, especially if older stock is already competing for the same buyers.

The table applies the same percentage decline to all four categories, rounds projected sales down to whole units, and assumes the advance order is the only stock available. The dollar figure measures purchase cost still tied up at day 90.

| Decline from latest winter sales | Guides left | Puzzles left | Cookbooks left | Graphic novels left | Cash tied up |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 25% | 1 | 0 | 0 | 0 | $9 |
| 40% | 8 | 0 | 0 | 0 | $72 |
| 60% | 17 | 0 | 0 | 5 | $203 |

These are category-level scenarios. Carryover stock can leave more of the new order unsold, and a poor title mix can create leftovers even when category sales are strong enough to absorb the planned quantity. A drop concentrated in local travel or visitor traffic would put more pressure on guides than the across-the-board scenarios suggest. The stockout requests make a case for ordering deeper into proven guide titles, but they tell the shop little about how those titles will fare if visitor demand changes.

If the shop already sees weaker demand for guides before placing the order, a second $900 mix is **28 guides, 18 puzzles, 10 cookbooks, and 29 graphic novels**. It trades six guides for four puzzles and one graphic novel. Under the 40% decline scenario, that mix would leave two guides costing $18, compared with eight guides costing $72 under the recommended order. The tradeoff is six fewer guides available in the category that had 15 stockout requests last winter.

On the two winters of evidence, I would place the 34-guide order. The guides’ near-complete sell-through and rising requests justify the extra copies, and the graphic novel order gives the shop meaningful depth in its fastest-growing category by unit sales. The final title choices should follow the request records and the stock already on the shelf. That is where the shop can do the most to turn this $900 into sales within the winter window.
